questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Explicit Cartesian Equation
questions.problem: Find a vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ that parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z={x}^{3}-xy.$
questions.worked_solution:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=x\,i+y\,j+z\,k=x\,i+y\,j+({x}^{3}-xy)\,k.
$$

Now, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+({u}^{3}-uv)\,k
$$

questions.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\text{_____}\,k
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
${x}^{2}y-{z}^{3}=3.$ 
 What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y-{z}^{3} & =3 \\ {z}^{3} & ={x}^{2}y-3 \\ z & =\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}y-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=x\,i+y\,j+z\,k=x\,i+y\,j+\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}y-3}\,k.
$$

   

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}v-3}\,k
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}v-3}.$

$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
$2x-3y+\sqrt[3]{2z}=0.$
 What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3y+\sqrt[3]{2z} & =0 \\ \sqrt[3]{2z} & =3y-2x \\ z & =\frac{(3y-2x)^{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=x\,i+y\,j+z\,k=x\,i+y\,j+\frac{(3y-2x)^{3}}{2}\,k.
$$

 

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=u\,i+v\,j+\frac{(3v-2u)^{3}}{2}\,k
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\frac{(3v-2u)^{3}}{2}.$

questions.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
${x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-{z}^{2}=1$
for $z>0.$ What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {z}^{2} & ={x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1 \\ z & =\sqrt{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since we are given that $z>0.$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨x,\,y,\,\sqrt{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-1}⟩.
$$

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\sqrt{{u}^{3}+{v}^{3}-1}⟩
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\sqrt{{u}^{3}+{v}^{3}-1}.$

**Note:** The parametrization is well-defined for $u$ and $v$ such that ${u}^{3}+{v}^{3}-1\ge 0.$

questions.problem:
$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_____},\,2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(r,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as 
$z=2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$
What is the second component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
f=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩.
$$

Finally, substituting $z=2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain the parametrization

$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩.
$$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

questions.problem:
$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(r,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as 
$\frac{{z}^{2}}{{r}^{4}}={sin}^{2}⁡2\theta $
for $z\ge 0$ and $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ What is the third component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(r,\theta ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{z}^{2}}{{r}^{4}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡2\theta  \\ {z}^{2} & ={r}^{4}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta  \\ z & ={r}^{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta | \\ z & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since we are given that $z\ge 0.$ Also, we drop the absolute value bars because $\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \ge 0$ for  $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$  

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
f=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩.
$$

Finally, substituting $z={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ we obtain

$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ⟩.
$$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is ${r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined in Spherical Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\text{ _____ }⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ)$ parametrizes the surface defined in spherical polar coordinates as 
$ϕ=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$
What is the third component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $\rho =f(\theta ,ϕ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \rho  & =\frac{ϕ}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
f=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.
$$

Finally, substituting $\rho =\frac{ϕ}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨\frac{ϕ}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{ϕ}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{ϕ}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $ϕ\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $ϕ{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined in Spherical Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨\text{_____},\,ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ)$ parametrizes the surface defined in spherical polar coordinates as 
$\rho =ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$
What is the first component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
f=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.
$$

Finally, substituting $\rho =ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Explicit Cartesian Equation
canonical_examples.problem: Find a vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ that parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=y^5-x^2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = x \, \mathbf{i} + y \, \mathbf{j} + z \, \mathbf{k} = x \, \mathbf{i} + y \, \mathbf{j} + \big(y^5-x^2\big) \, \mathbf{k}.
$$

Now, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = u \, \mathbf{i} + v \, \mathbf{j} + \big(v^5-u^2\big) \, \mathbf{k}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Implicit Cartesian Equation
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) =\big\langle u, \: v, \:  \text{_____} \big\rangle
$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
$x^2z-2y+z=6.$
 What is the third component of $\mathbf{r}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}z-2y+z & =6 \\ ({x}^{2}+1)z & =6+2y \\ z & =\frac{2(y+3)}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \left\langle x, \: y, \: \dfrac{2(y+3)}{x^2+1} \right\rangle.
$$

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) =\left\langle u, \: v, \:  {\color{black}\dfrac{2(v+3)}{u^2+1}} \right\rangle
$$

 

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{r}$ is ${\color{black}\dfrac{2(v+3)}{u^2+1}}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined in Cylindrical Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\big\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle
$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(r,\theta)$ parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as 
${r^2}-4z^2=0$
for $z \geq 0.$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{f}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(r,\theta)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2}-4{z}^{2} & =0 \\ 4{z}^{2} & ={r}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & =\frac{{r}^{2}}{4} \\ z & =\frac{r}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since we are given that $z\geq 0.$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
\mathbf{f} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \big\langle r\cos\theta, \: r\sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle.
$$

Finally, substituting $z= \dfrac r2,$ we obtain

$$
\mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\left\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: {\color{black}  \dfrac r2} \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{black}  \dfrac r2}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined in Spherical Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: \theta \sin\theta \sin^2 \phi, \: \theta \sin\phi \cos\phi \big\rangle
$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)$ parametrizes the surface defined in spherical polar coordinates as 
$\rho=\theta \sin{\phi}.$
What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad
y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 
z = \rho\cos\phi
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
\mathbf{f} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \big\langle \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho\cos\phi \big\rangle.
$$

Finally, substituting $\rho=\theta \sin{\phi},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ,\,\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ,\,\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{black}\theta \cos\theta \sin^2 \phi}.$
